text: I'll aim for a concise response, around 300 words.

Rivers are among the oldest storytellers on Earth. Long before people wrote anything down, rivers were carving canyons, shaping valleys, and drawing lines across continents. The Colorado River spent roughly six million years cutting the Grand Canyon. The Nile has flooded and pulled back on a steady rhythm for millennia, and that rhythm made one of history's great civilizations possible.

At its simplest, a river is water following gravity. Rain falls on high ground, snow melts on mountain peaks, and springs rise from underground. The water gathers into rivulets and streams, and they join into something larger. Each river drains a watershed, an area of land whose water all flows toward the same channel. The Amazon's watershed covers about 40 percent of South America. It carries more water than the next several largest rivers combined.

Rivers are also engines of life. Their banks hold some of the richest ecosystems on the planet. Wetlands filter pollutants, deltas shelter young fish, and floodplains spread fertile silt across farmland. Salmon swim thousands of miles upstream to spawn in the gravel beds where they hatched, and their bodies feed forests when they die. Herons, otters, dragonflies, and countless microorganisms all depend on moving fresh water.

People have always settled near rivers. Mesopotamia grew up between the Tigris and the Euphrates, and its name means "land between rivers." Cities like London, Cairo, Varanasi, and New Orleans owe their existence to rivers that brought trade, drinking water, and transport. Rivers have also marked borders, inspired religions, and filled poetry, from Heraclitus's saying that no one steps in the same river twice to Langston Hughes's "The Negro Speaks of Rivers."

Today many rivers are under strain. Dams break up their flow, pollution degrades their water, and climate change is shifting the snowmelt and rainfall that feed them. Restoration work, such as removing old dams and reconnecting floodplains, shows that rivers can recover when given room.

A river is never finished. It keeps moving and changing, and it carries the past toward the sea.
